messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Catastrophising Others: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform

Vignette:
When Amina was in her twenties, she fled political violence in her East African home country after armed men began moving through her region, taking people from villages and forcing them to carry supplies and follow orders at gunpoint. What stayed with her most sharply was not a single image but the absolute loss of choice. She remembered being marched with others along rough, green terrain outside the village, surrounded by brush and open land that should have looked ordinary and beautiful, and feeling that her body no longer belonged to her. Men with weapons told people when to move, where to stand, when to be silent. Uniforms and commands became fused in her mind with immediate danger. She eventually escaped and made her way through refugee channels to the United States, where she built a life that, on the surface, looked orderly and self-directed.

Over the decades, Amina became a financial analyst, a role she valued partly because it rewarded planning, precision, and control. She lived alone and prided herself on managing without depending on anyone. Colleagues knew her as careful and composed. What they did not see was how quickly that composure narrowed when she felt cornered. If a supervisor spoke in a clipped, directive tone or told her she “had to” do something on short notice, she felt a surge of alarm that seemed larger than the moment. She would not describe it as anger so much as a visceral recoil: a conviction that once someone else took control, terrible things could follow. She became especially tense around security personnel in her office building and avoided interactions with police whenever possible, even ordinary ones. If officers were standing near the entrance or on the subway platform, she would wait, reroute, or leave altogether. The sight of a uniformed authority figure brought with it the same sense she had known years ago, that compliance was not safe and refusal was impossible.

Her avoidance had gradually shaped her life. At work she steered away from disagreement, even when she believed an analysis was wrong or a decision unwise. In meetings she would soften, withdraw, or say she was “fine with whatever the team decides,” because confrontation felt dangerous the moment voices sharpened or hierarchy became explicit. Over time this cost her professionally. Less experienced coworkers advanced into more visible roles while Amina stayed in the background, reliable but unseen. She told herself this was preferable to attracting scrutiny. She also organized her days to minimize contact with authority figures, choosing entrances with less security presence, postponing errands if police were nearby, and avoiding any setting where she might be told what to do.

Outside work, she had become preoccupied with the safety of the few people she was close to, especially relatives and friends from her immigrant community. If someone did not answer a call or text, her mind jumped quickly to the worst possibilities: detention, violence, an accident, some sudden irrevocable loss. She would replay imagined scenarios in detail and keep calling until she heard back. She knew other people experienced these reactions as excessive, but to her it felt reckless not to anticipate disaster. The world had once changed without warning; she was certain it could do so again at any moment.

One reason she had so few restorative outlets was that she increasingly avoided natural settings. Friends invited her on walks in local parks or weekend picnics, and she almost always declined. It was not “nature” in any abstract sense that unsettled her, but a specific kind of landscape: open green space, brush, uneven ground, the smell of earth after heat. Those environments pulled her back toward the place where armed men had ordered bodies into lines and made movement a matter of survival. Even a company retreat held at a conference center near wooded trails left her shaken. She stayed inside as much as possible, telling coworkers she had emails to catch up on.

By the time she sought help at 63, these patterns had tightened around her. The immediate prompt was a conflict at work that she did not manage to avoid: a senior manager abruptly reassigned one of her projects and instructed her to follow a new reporting structure. Amina agreed outwardly, then spent the night overwhelmed, unable to stop thinking not only about her own vulnerability but about her niece, who had been traveling and was temporarily unreachable. The next morning, seeing police officers outside her office building, she froze on the sidewalk and could not make herself go in. It frightened her that her life had become so constricted after so many years of trying to stay safe through discipline and caution. In coming to treatment, what she most hoped for was not to become carefree, which seemed impossible, but to move through her days without feeling instantly overrun by command, uniforms, or the possibility of catastrophe. What frightened her most was that if she loosened her vigilance even slightly, she or someone she loved would pay for it.
